opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point is just a comparison of the numbers. A child is exposed to something like tens of millions of words in the first several years of life, maybe on the order of a hundred million by the time they're a teenager. The models that we're impressed by today are trained on hundreds of billions or trillions of words. So that's a difference of several orders of magnitude. And yet, by the time children are five or six, they've figured out the core of the grammar of their language. They know how to form questions, they know how agreement works, they generalize to sentences they've never heard before in a pretty systematic way.

So if you take a model and train it on a human-scale amount of data, what you typically find is that it does learn a lot, but it doesn't generalize the way people do. It picks up on surface statistics, on linear order and word co-occurrence, rather than on the hierarchical structure that seems to underlie human language. We've seen this in a number of experiments, for example with things like question formation in English, where there's an ambiguity in the training data between a linear rule and a hierarchical rule, and children reliably go for the hierarchical one. Neural networks trained from scratch often don't, or they only do it with much more data.

And to me, that gap tells you something. The way I think about it is that every learner has to bring something to the problem. The data alone never fully determines how you should generalize. There are always many hypotheses consistent with what you've seen. What decides between them is the learner's inductive biases. Humans seem to have biases that lead them, quickly and fairly consistently, to the right kinds of generalizations. Current architectures like the transformer have biases too, but they're apparently not the same ones, and they seem to be weaker in the relevant sense. So the model compensates with massive amounts of data.

Now, you might ask, why does it matter? If we can just train on more data, who cares? I think there are a few reasons. One is scientific. If we want to use these models as models of human language acquisition, to say something about what's learnable from the input a child actually gets, then we need them to learn in a human-like regime. Otherwise the conclusions don't transfer. The other reason is more practical. There are lots of languages and lots of domains where you simply don't have trillions of words. And even in English, the kind of robust, systematic generalization you get from the right biases is something you'd want in a system you can rely on, especially out of distribution.

I should say I don't think this means the biases have to be some specific innate grammar hardwired in. It's an open question what form they should take. It could be architectural, it could come from pretraining on some other kind of data or task, it could come from grounding or interaction, the way children learn in a social, perceptual context rather than from a stream of text. Part of what I find exciting is that we can now actually test these hypotheses empirically, by changing the learner and seeing whether it starts generalizing more like a person does with a person's amount of data.

r001.rationale: It says networks trained from scratch often fail to choose the hierarchical question rule, but does not state that a network failed to transform declarative sentences into questions using the amount of evidence in child-directed speech.

r002.rationale: It says networks may learn the hierarchical question rule “with much more data,” describing eventual learning of question formation with substantially more evidence.

r003.rationale: It contrasts hierarchical structure with linear order, but does not identify operating on sentence trees rather than word sequences as a possible architectural bias.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point for me is just a very basic quantitative mismatch. A child who's acquiring their first language hears something on the order of tens of millions of words by the time they're, say, five or six. The estimates vary, but even generous ones put it in the low tens of millions. And yet by that age children have a pretty solid grasp of the syntax of their language. They can form questions correctly, they handle agreement across long dependencies, they generalize to sentence structures they've never heard before. They don't do all of this perfectly, but they do it remarkably well.

Now compare that to what we need to train a language model to reach a comparable level of grammatical competence. We're talking about hundreds of billions or trillions of tokens, which is several orders of magnitude more than any human sees in a lifetime. And this is text, which is already much cleaner and more varied than the child-directed speech a kid actually gets. So the models are getting a much larger and in some ways much better dataset and still needing far more of it.

To me that gap is a signal. If a learner reaches the target with a tiny fraction of the data, it must be bringing something to the problem that constrains the hypothesis space. That's what we mean by an inductive bias: it's whatever makes the learner prefer some generalizations over others before it has seen the evidence that would distinguish them. The classic example from the acquisition literature is hierarchical structure. When kids learn to form yes-no questions, they move the auxiliary that's structurally highest, not the first one that appears linearly, even though both rules are consistent with the vast majority of the sentences they hear. Children essentially never make the linear mistake. Standard neural models, when you train them on data of a realistic size, often do make that kind of mistake, or they're inconsistent about it. They have to be shown a lot of disambiguating examples before they settle on the hierarchical generalization.

So my view isn't that neural networks are the wrong kind of system, or that they can't learn language. Clearly they can, if you give them enough data. The point is more that if you want a model to be a plausible account of human learning, or even just if you want a model that's more data-efficient, you have to ask what biases the learner needs so that the hierarchical generalization is the natural one rather than something it has to be dragged to. That could come from architecture, it could come from the training objective, it could even be something like pretraining on a synthetic structured language before exposing the model to real text. We've played with several of those. But the big-picture claim is simply that data alone, at human scale, doesn't seem to be enough, and the model has to make up the difference somehow.

r001.rationale: The response says children learn hierarchical question formation from limited child-directed input, while standard neural models trained at realistic data sizes often make the linear auxiliary-selection error.

r002.rationale: It says neural networks can learn language with enough data and that models need many more disambiguating examples before settling on the hierarchical question-forming generalization.

r003.rationale: The response names hierarchical structure and architecture as possible sources of bias, but does not identify operating on sentence trees rather than word sequences.

astra-6.text:
Well, the striking thing is that children learn language from much less data than we typically use to train language models. So if our goal is to explain how humans acquire language, getting good performance after training on an enormous amount of text doesn’t really answer the question. We want to know what makes learning possible with the input a child actually receives.

Inductive biases are the assumptions that allow a learner to generalize beyond the examples it has seen. A limited amount of data is compatible with lots of different generalizations, and some of those will work much better than others. If the learner has some preference for the right kinds of generalizations, it doesn’t need to see every construction over and over again.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we have to build in a detailed theory of grammar. The useful biases could be more general, or they could come from the way children learn through perception and interaction. The question is which assumptions actually help a model learn language from a realistic amount of experience. That’s something we can try to test experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses children’s limited language input generally, but does not state that a neural network failed to learn English question formation from child-directed speech.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a neural network eventually learns question formation with substantially more training evidence.

r003.rationale: It mentions inductive biases in general but does not identify sentence trees rather than word sequences as a possible architectural bias.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the motivation is that children learn language from much less data than we typically train language models on. So if our goal is to explain how humans acquire language, a model that succeeds only after seeing billions or trillions of words leaves something important unexplained.

An inductive bias is something that helps a learner choose among the many generalizations compatible with its experience. For example, languages have hierarchical structure, and a learner that is predisposed to look for that structure may need fewer examples than one that has to discover it from scratch.

That doesn’t necessarily mean we should build in a complete grammar. The relevant biases could come from the architecture, the learning procedure, or the fact that children learn language while interacting with people and the physical world. The question is which of those ingredients allow a model to learn the right generalizations from a human-sized amount of experience. If a model can do that without explicitly linguistic biases, that would also be a very interesting result.

r001.rationale: The response discusses children’s limited language data and inductive biases generally, but does not state that a neural network failed to form English questions from child-directed speech.

r002.rationale: It does not say the network eventually learned question formation with substantially more evidence.

r003.rationale: It mentions hierarchical structure generally, but does not identify operating on sentence trees rather than word sequences as a possible architectural bias.
